title: CrashLoopBackOff / pod keeps restarting
summary: Use the previous container state and events to find the failure before restarting again.

steps.title: Confirm restart pattern
steps.look: Check STATUS and whether RESTARTS is increasing.

steps.title: Read previous container logs
steps.look: Look for the first fatal startup/config/dependency error.

steps.title: Inspect termination state
steps.look: Read Last State, Reason, Exit Code and events.

steps.title: Check current metrics if available
steps.look: OOM or sustained memory pressure may point to memory investigation.

likely_causes: For “CrashLoopBackOff / pod keeps restarting”: the process exits because of startup/configuration/dependency failure.
OOM, probe, signal, lifecycle hook or runtime behavior terminates the container.
Image entrypoint/command/args are incompatible with the workload.
verification: RESTARTS stays stable through the normal workload window.
Container remains Ready without a new termination state.
The original startup/request no longer reproduces the crash.
escalation: Current and --previous logs
lastState reason/exitCode/signal/timestamps
Image/command/args/env/resources and Pod events

branches.when: lastState is OOMKilled or exit 137
branches.then: Follow the memory path before changing restart behavior.

branches.when: --previous logs show startup/dependency error
branches.then: Fix that exact dependency/configuration path.

branches.when: Logs are empty or exit is immediate
branches.then: Inspect command/args, entrypoint, working directory and permissions.

example.root_cause: The application process exits during startup because required runtime configuration is missing.
example.remediation: Correct the owning Deployment/Secret/ConfigMap reference in source control, reconcile it, then watch the rollout rather than repeatedly restarting the Pod.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: CrashLoopBackOff is the restart backoff symptom; previous-container logs and termination state reveal the actual application failure.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: For “CrashLoopBackOff / pod keeps restarting”: the process exits because of startup/configuration/dependency failure.
OOM, probe, signal, lifecycle hook or runtime behavior terminates the container.
The visible symptom may be secondary, so preserve state and verify the failing layer before changing anything.
ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.
example.safety_and_rollback: Before a state-changing action, preserve the before-state, confirm the exact target/environment, identify the rollback path, and follow the project's change process. Commands shown in the walkthrough are illustrative; destructive remediation is intentionally not auto-executed.
success_criteria: The original symptom no longer reproduces.
The corrected state remains healthy through the same restart/load/failure window.
Fresh logs/events/status no longer contain the original failure signature.
example.transferable_pattern: Kubernetes pattern: start from the observable symptom, identify the first concrete mismatch in the Pods path, prove the responsible layer with a second piece of evidence, correct the source of truth, then verify using the original reproduction.

title: Service has no ready backends / no endpoints
summary: Use EndpointSlice, selectors and readiness to find why a Service has no usable backends.

steps.title: Inspect Service selector and ports
steps.look: Note Selector, Port and TargetPort.

steps.title: Check EndpointSlices
steps.look: If no endpoint addresses are present, focus on selector/readiness.

steps.title: Compare pod labels
steps.look: Selectors must match intended pod labels.

steps.title: Check pod readiness
steps.look: Pods that are not Ready need readiness/application investigation.

likely_causes: For “Service has no ready backends / no endpoints”: service selector does not select the intended Ready Pods.
port/targetPort/protocol does not match the application listener.
Traffic policy, NetworkPolicy or the service data plane prevents traffic reaching healthy endpoints.
verification: EndpointSlices contain expected Ready Pod IPs/ports.
Direct Pod and Service tests both succeed from the same client.
Original request succeeds across multiple backends.
escalation: Service YAML/selectors/ports
EndpointSlice readiness and Pod labels
Direct-Pod vs Service test plus policies/traffic settings

branches.when: EndpointSlices are empty
branches.then: Compare Service selectors with Pod labels/readiness.

branches.when: Direct Pod IP works but Service IP fails
branches.then: Focus on Service port mapping/traffic policy/data plane.

branches.when: Internal Service works but external path fails
branches.then: Move to NodePort/LB/externalTrafficPolicy and external health checks.

summary: Find readiness probe or application dependency failures.

steps.title: Check readiness columns

likely_causes: A readiness probe is failing because the endpoint/port/command is wrong or the application/dependency is not healthy.
A custom readinessGate condition is false or never updated by the responsible controller.
The container is running but cannot serve traffic because of dependency, listener, certificate, configuration or resource-pressure problems.
verification: READY reaches the intended container count and remains stable.
Pod Ready condition stays True across several probe periods.
Service EndpointSlices mark the Pod ready and the application request succeeds.
escalation: Pod conditions/readinessGates and describe events
Probe configuration plus application logs
EndpointSlice readiness and dependency/listener evidence

example.root_cause: The application is running but its readiness endpoint rejects traffic while a required dependency is unavailable.
example.remediation: Restore the dependency or correct the readiness design/configuration; do not bypass readiness merely to make the Pod appear healthy.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: Running and Ready are different states: readiness controls whether the Pod should receive Service traffic.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: A readiness probe is failing because the endpoint/port/command is wrong or the application/dependency is not healthy.
A custom readinessGate condition is false or never updated by the responsible controller.

ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.

title: Secret or ConfigMap change not reflected

steps.title: Inspect pod spec
steps.look: Look at env/envFrom and volume mounts.

steps.title: Check ConfigMaps
steps.look: Confirm referenced object names.

likely_causes: The value is consumed through environment variables, which are fixed at container start and require Pod recreation to change.

verification: Confirm the live Pod consumes the expected object/key and value delivery mechanism.
Verify the application sees the new value after the appropriate refresh/restart behavior.
Confirm newly created Pods reference the intended ConfigMap/Secret revision/name.
escalation: Pod env/envFrom/volume/volumeMount references
ConfigMap/Secret metadata and key names with secret values redacted
Mounted-file timestamp/content hash or rollout revision showing when consumers changed

likely_causes: The StatefulSet selector/labels no longer match the intended workload or peer set.

branches.then: Trace mutation/Helm/GitOps/controller ownership before editing the live object.

title: Service status changed unexpectedly
summary: Capture live state, conditions and events for the Service.

steps.title: Capture YAML
steps.look: Review generation, status and metadata.

steps.title: Describe resource
steps.look: Read conditions and related events.

steps.title: Check recent events
steps.look: Look for events near the time behavior changed.

likely_causes: The Service spec, dependency or controller-observed state changed and produced a different status/condition.
A rollout, reschedule, policy, quota, endpoint, storage or node event changed the Service's effective state without an obvious manifest edit.
The object was recreated or reconciled by another actor, so status now reflects a newer generation or dependency state.
verification: Confirm Service conditions/status stabilize at the intended state.
Confirm no new unexpected generation/UID/controller changes occur during the observation window.
Repeat the workload path that depends on this resource and verify normal behavior.
escalation: Current and previous Service YAML/status if available
metadata.generation, UID, managedFields and events
Owning-controller logs and dependency changes around the first status transition

branches.when: metadata.generation changed
branches.then: Diff the live spec/managedFields against the last known-good revision and identify the actor.

branches.when: generation is unchanged but status changed
branches.then: Inspect conditions/events and the owning controller/dependencies; this is likely environmental or reconciliation-driven.

branches.when: UID changed
branches.then: Treat it as object recreation and trace the controller/release that recreated it.

example.root_cause: The Service selector does not match the ready backend Pod labels, so no usable endpoint is published.
example.remediation: Align the Service selector with the workload's stable labels in the owning manifests and verify EndpointSlice population.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: A healthy Pod does not receive Service traffic unless selector matching and EndpointSlice readiness also line up.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: The Service spec, dependency or controller-observed state changed and produced a different status/condition.
A rollout, reschedule, policy, quota, endpoint, storage or node event changed the Service's effective state without an obvious manifest edit.
The visible symptom may be secondary, so preserve state and verify the failing layer before changing anything.
ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.
example.safety_and_rollback: Before a state-changing action, preserve the before-state, confirm the exact target/environment, identify the rollback path, and follow the project's change process. Commands shown in the walkthrough are illustrative; destructive remediation is intentionally not auto-executed.
success_criteria: The original symptom no longer reproduces.
The corrected state remains healthy through the same restart/load/failure window.
Fresh logs/events/status no longer contain the original failure signature.
example.transferable_pattern: Kubernetes pattern: start from the observable symptom, identify the first concrete mismatch in the Networking path, prove the responsible layer with a second piece of evidence, correct the source of truth, then verify using the original reproduction.

title: Service labels or selectors look wrong
summary: Inspect labels/selectors around the Service before editing metadata.

steps.title: Show labels
steps.look: Record current labels.

steps.title: Inspect full YAML
steps.look: Review selector-related fields that vary by resource type.

steps.title: Inspect related pods
steps.look: Compare intended workload labels where relevant.

likely_causes: The Service selector/labels no longer match the intended workload or peer set.
A rollout/template/Helm/GitOps change altered labels on one side but not the selector/reference on the other.
Overlapping or overly broad labels select unintended objects, while missing labels exclude the expected objects.
verification: Evaluate the selector against live labels and confirm only the intended objects match.
Confirm newly created Pods/resources inherit the corrected labels from their owning template.
Repeat the original routing/policy/controller behavior and verify the selector now produces the intended result.
escalation: Live Service selector/labels
Target object labels plus owning workload template labels
Source manifest/Helm/GitOps revision or managedFields showing who changed metadata

branches.when: Selector matches zero intended objects
branches.then: Compare selector key/value pairs with live target labels and the workload template that creates them.

branches.when: Selector matches both intended and unintended objects
branches.then: Tighten the label contract in source configuration; do not patch individual Pods as a permanent fix.

branches.when: Live labels differ from source manifest
branches.then: Trace mutation/Helm/GitOps/controller ownership before editing the live object.

title: NetworkPolicy labels or selectors look wrong
summary: Inspect labels/selectors around the NetworkPolicy before editing metadata.

steps.title: Show labels
steps.look: Record current labels.

steps.title: Inspect full YAML
steps.look: Review selector-related fields that vary by resource type.

steps.title: Inspect related pods
steps.look: Compare intended workload labels where relevant.

likely_causes: The NetworkPolicy selector/labels no longer match the intended workload or peer set.
A rollout/template/Helm/GitOps change altered labels on one side but not the selector/reference on the other.
Overlapping or overly broad labels select unintended objects, while missing labels exclude the expected objects.
verification: Evaluate the selector against live labels and confirm only the intended objects match.
Confirm newly created Pods/resources inherit the corrected labels from their owning template.
Repeat the original routing/policy/controller behavior and verify the selector now produces the intended result.
escalation: Live NetworkPolicy selector/labels
Target object labels plus owning workload template labels
Source manifest/Helm/GitOps revision or managedFields showing who changed metadata

branches.when: Selector matches zero intended objects
branches.then: Compare selector key/value pairs with live target labels and the workload template that creates them.

branches.when: Selector matches both intended and unintended objects
branches.then: Tighten the label contract in source configuration; do not patch individual Pods as a permanent fix.

branches.when: Live labels differ from source manifest
branches.then: Trace mutation/Helm/GitOps/controller ownership before editing the live object.

example.remediation: Correct the owning manifest/controller/dependency at its source, apply the minimum safe change, and re-run the same diagnostic checks.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: Use the first concrete condition/event mismatch to narrow the incident; avoid changing several Kubernetes layers at once.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.

title: CronJob labels or selectors look wrong
summary: Inspect labels/selectors around the CronJob before editing metadata.

steps.title: Show labels
steps.look: Record current labels.

steps.title: Inspect full YAML
steps.look: Review selector-related fields that vary by resource type.

steps.title: Inspect related pods
steps.look: Compare intended workload labels where relevant.

likely_causes: The CronJob selector/labels no longer match the intended workload or peer set.
A rollout/template/Helm/GitOps change altered labels on one side but not the selector/reference on the other.
Overlapping or overly broad labels select unintended objects, while missing labels exclude the expected objects.
verification: Evaluate the selector against live labels and confirm only the intended objects match.
Confirm newly created Pods/resources inherit the corrected labels from their owning template.
Repeat the original routing/policy/controller behavior and verify the selector now produces the intended result.
escalation: Live CronJob selector/labels
Target object labels plus owning workload template labels
Source manifest/Helm/GitOps revision or managedFields showing who changed metadata

branches.when: Selector matches zero intended objects
branches.then: Compare selector key/value pairs with live target labels and the workload template that creates them.

branches.when: Selector matches both intended and unintended objects
branches.then: Tighten the label contract in source configuration; do not patch individual Pods as a permanent fix.

branches.when: Live labels differ from source manifest
branches.then: Trace mutation/Helm/GitOps/controller ownership before editing the live object.

title: ConfigMap labels or selectors look wrong
summary: Inspect labels/selectors around the ConfigMap before editing metadata.

steps.title: Show labels
steps.look: Record current labels.

steps.title: Inspect full YAML
steps.look: Review selector-related fields that vary by resource type.

steps.title: Inspect related pods
steps.look: Compare intended workload labels where relevant.

likely_causes: The ConfigMap selector/labels no longer match the intended workload or peer set.
A rollout/template/Helm/GitOps change altered labels on one side but not the selector/reference on the other.
Overlapping or overly broad labels select unintended objects, while missing labels exclude the expected objects.
verification: Evaluate the selector against live labels and confirm only the intended objects match.
Confirm newly created Pods/resources inherit the corrected labels from their owning template.
Repeat the original routing/policy/controller behavior and verify the selector now produces the intended result.
escalation: Live ConfigMap selector/labels
Target object labels plus owning workload template labels
Source manifest/Helm/GitOps revision or managedFields showing who changed metadata

branches.when: Selector matches zero intended objects
branches.then: Compare selector key/value pairs with live target labels and the workload template that creates them.

branches.when: Selector matches both intended and unintended objects
branches.then: Tighten the label contract in source configuration; do not patch individual Pods as a permanent fix.

branches.when: Live labels differ from source manifest
branches.then: Trace mutation/Helm/GitOps/controller ownership before editing the live object.

example.incident: Production alert: ConfigMap labels or selectors look wrong. An engineer needs to restore service without guessing or making broad changes.

timeline.output:
Observed state for ConfigMap labels or selectors look wrong:
status/condition differs from expected healthy state.
timeline.reasoning: Start with live state and preserve the exact status/error before making any change.

timeline.command: kubectl get configmap checkout-api -n production -o yaml
timeline.output: Warning  ReconcileError  2m  controller  dependency or configuration check failed
timeline.reasoning: Use the first concrete condition, event or termination detail to decide which layer owns the failure.

timeline.output: Live object and related dependency inspected; one effective value differs from the intended configuration.
timeline.reasoning: Check the directly related configuration/dependency so the remediation is based on evidence, not the top-level symptom.

example.root_cause: The walkthrough isolates “ConfigMap labels or selectors look wrong” to the first live state/dependency that differs from the intended Kubernetes configuration.
example.remediation: Correct the owning manifest/controller/dependency at its source, apply the minimum safe change, and re-run the same diagnostic checks.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: Use the first concrete condition/event mismatch to narrow the incident; avoid changing several Kubernetes layers at once.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: The ConfigMap selector/labels no longer match the intended workload or peer set.
A rollout/template/Helm/GitOps change altered labels on one side but not the selector/reference on the other.
The visible symptom may be secondary, so preserve state and verify the failing layer before changing anything.
ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.
example.safety_and_rollback: Before a state-changing action, preserve the before-state, confirm the exact target/environment, identify the rollback path, and follow the project's change process. Commands shown in the walkthrough are illustrative; destructive remediation is intentionally not auto-executed.
success_criteria: The original symptom no longer reproduces.
The corrected state remains healthy through the same restart/load/failure window.
Fresh logs/events/status no longer contain the original failure signature.
example.transferable_pattern: Kubernetes pattern: start from the observable symptom, identify the first concrete mismatch in the Configuration path, prove the responsible layer with a second piece of evidence, correct the source of truth, then verify using the original reproduction.

title: Secret not found or wrong namespace
summary: Confirm the Secret name and namespace before changing anything.

steps.title: List matching resource names
steps.look: Check spelling and whether the object exists.

steps.title: Search across namespaces
steps.look: If present elsewhere, confirm the intended project/environment before proceeding.

steps.title: Check permission
steps.look: A forbidden result can look like an access problem rather than absence.

likely_causes: Secret is absent from the namespace/context currently targeted by kubectl.
The object exists under a different name, namespace or cluster/context than the one being queried.
The object was renamed, deleted, recreated, or is generated by another controller/release and the expected reference is stale.
verification: Query the intended namespace/context and confirm the expected Secret is returned.
Confirm dependent workloads/references now resolve the same Secret name and scope.
Repeat the original operation and verify the NotFound error is gone.
escalation: kubectl current-context plus active namespace
Namespaced listing/YAML for the expected Secret
Owner/release/GitOps reference or deletion event if the object disappeared

branches.when: `kubectl get` cannot find the Secret in the expected namespace
branches.then: Confirm current context and namespace, then list the resource type before changing anything.

branches.when: The Secret exists in another namespace/context
branches.then: Correct the target/reference rather than recreating a duplicate object.

branches.when: The object truly no longer exists
branches.then: Trace its owning controller, release, GitOps source or creation workflow before restoring it.

title: Secret status changed unexpectedly
summary: Capture live state, conditions and events for the Secret.

steps.title: Capture YAML
steps.look: Review generation, status and metadata.

steps.title: Describe resource
steps.look: Read conditions and related events.

steps.title: Check recent events
steps.look: Look for events near the time behavior changed.

likely_causes: The Secret spec, dependency or controller-observed state changed and produced a different status/condition.
A rollout, reschedule, policy, quota, endpoint, storage or node event changed the Secret's effective state without an obvious manifest edit.
The object was recreated or reconciled by another actor, so status now reflects a newer generation or dependency state.
verification: Confirm Secret conditions/status stabilize at the intended state.
Confirm no new unexpected generation/UID/controller changes occur during the observation window.
Repeat the workload path that depends on this resource and verify normal behavior.
escalation: Current and previous Secret YAML/status if available
metadata.generation, UID, managedFields and events
Owning-controller logs and dependency changes around the first status transition

branches.when: metadata.generation changed
branches.then: Diff the live spec/managedFields against the last known-good revision and identify the actor.

branches.then: Treat it as object recreation and trace the controller/release that recreated it.

example.root_cause: The walkthrough isolates “Secret status changed unexpectedly” to the first live state/dependency that differs from the intended Kubernetes configuration.
example.remediation: Correct the owning manifest/controller/dependency at its source, apply the minimum safe change, and re-run the same diagnostic checks.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: Use the first concrete condition/event mismatch to narrow the incident; avoid changing several Kubernetes layers at once.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: The Secret spec, dependency or controller-observed state changed and produced a different status/condition.
A rollout, reschedule, policy, quota, endpoint, storage or node event changed the Secret's effective state without an obvious manifest edit.
The visible symptom may be secondary, so preserve state and verify the failing layer before changing anything.
ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.
example.safety_and_rollback: Before a state-changing action, preserve the before-state, confirm the exact target/environment, identify the rollback path, and follow the project's change process. Commands shown in the walkthrough are illustrative; destructive remediation is intentionally not auto-executed.
success_criteria: The original symptom no longer reproduces.

Fresh logs/events/status no longer contain the original failure signature.

title: Secret labels or selectors look wrong
summary: Inspect labels/selectors around the Secret before editing metadata.

steps.title: Show labels
steps.look: Record current labels.

steps.title: Inspect full YAML
steps.look: Review selector-related fields that vary by resource type.

steps.title: Inspect related pods
steps.look: Compare intended workload labels where relevant.

likely_causes: The Secret selector/labels no longer match the intended workload or peer set.
A rollout/template/Helm/GitOps change altered labels on one side but not the selector/reference on the other.
Overlapping or overly broad labels select unintended objects, while missing labels exclude the expected objects.
verification: Evaluate the selector against live labels and confirm only the intended objects match.
Confirm newly created Pods/resources inherit the corrected labels from their owning template.
Repeat the original routing/policy/controller behavior and verify the selector now produces the intended result.
escalation: Live Secret selector/labels
Target object labels plus owning workload template labels
Source manifest/Helm/GitOps revision or managedFields showing who changed metadata

branches.when: Selector matches zero intended objects
branches.then: Compare selector key/value pairs with live target labels and the workload template that creates them.

branches.when: Selector matches both intended and unintended objects
branches.then: Tighten the label contract in source configuration; do not patch individual Pods as a permanent fix.

branches.when: Live labels differ from source manifest
branches.then: Trace mutation/Helm/GitOps/controller ownership before editing the live object.

steps.title: Inspect node conditions
steps.look: Confirm DiskPressure=True and read related events/capacity information.

verification: Node Ready remains True and pressure conditions False.

Kubelet/runtime and workload networking/storage remain healthy over time.
escalation: Node Conditions/events and Lease timing
Kubelet/runtime logs

example.root_cause: The Service selector does not match the ready backend Pod labels, so no usable endpoint is published.
example.remediation: Align the Service selector with the workload's stable labels in the owning manifests and verify EndpointSlice population.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: A healthy Pod does not receive Service traffic unless selector matching and EndpointSlice readiness also line up.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: For “Service intermittently fails”: service selector does not select the intended Ready Pods.
port/targetPort/protocol does not match the application listener.
The visible symptom may be secondary, so preserve state and verify the failing layer before changing anything.
ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.
example.safety_and_rollback: Before a state-changing action, preserve the before-state, confirm the exact target/environment, identify the rollback path, and follow the project's change process. Commands shown in the walkthrough are illustrative; destructive remediation is intentionally not auto-executed.
success_criteria: The original symptom no longer reproduces.
The corrected state remains healthy through the same restart/load/failure window.
Fresh logs/events/status no longer contain the original failure signature.
example.transferable_pattern: Kubernetes pattern: start from the observable symptom, identify the first concrete mismatch in the Services & EndpointSlices path, prove the responsible layer with a second piece of evidence, correct the source of truth, then verify using the original reproduction.

steps.look: Look for SERVFAIL, timeout, loop, upstream or plugin errors.

steps.title: Inspect Pod state
steps.look: Confirm phase, readiness, restart count, Pod IP and node.

steps.title: Describe Pod
steps.look: Read container states, last state, reasons, conditions and events.

steps.title: Read current logs
steps.look: Find the first application/startup/dependency error.

steps.title: Read previous logs
steps.look: Use when containers restarted; previous logs often preserve the actual crash.

likely_causes: For “Node heartbeat delayed”: kubelet/runtime/networking is unhealthy or cannot report to the API server.
Disk/inode/memory/PID pressure triggers node conditions or eviction.
Certificates, heartbeat/lease, OS/runtime or local network/storage configuration is degraded.
verification: Node Ready remains True and pressure conditions False.
Affected Pods stop being evicted/recreated.
Kubelet/runtime and workload networking/storage remain healthy over time.
escalation: Node Conditions/events and Lease timing
Kubelet/runtime logs
Disk/inode/memory/PID usage and affected Pod inventory

branches.when: Ready is Unknown or heartbeat stale
branches.then: Check kubelet/runtime connectivity and Lease timing.

branches.when: A pressure condition is True
branches.then: Quantify that resource and identify consumers.

branches.when: Only one node is affected
branches.then: Compare runtime/CNI/DNS/filesystem/kubelet with a healthy node.

example.root_cause: The node is under disk/ephemeral-storage pressure and kubelet health has degraded.
example.remediation: Identify the disk consumer, restore node filesystem capacity safely, and confirm kubelet/node conditions recover before rescheduling workload.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: Node symptoms should be correlated with Conditions and kubelet events before touching individual Pods.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: For “Node heartbeat delayed”: kubelet/runtime/networking is unhealthy or cannot report to the API server.
Disk/inode/memory/PID pressure triggers node conditions or eviction.
The visible symptom may be secondary, so preserve state and verify the failing layer before changing anything.
ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.
example.safety_and_rollback: Before a state-changing action, preserve the before-state, confirm the exact target/environment, identify the rollback path, and follow the project's change process. Commands shown in the walkthrough are illustrative; destructive remediation is intentionally not auto-executed.
success_criteria: The original symptom no longer reproduces.
The corrected state remains healthy through the same restart/load/failure window.
Fresh logs/events/status no longer contain the original failure signature.
example.transferable_pattern: Kubernetes pattern: start from the observable symptom, identify the first concrete mismatch in the Nodes & Kubelet path, prove the responsible layer with a second piece of evidence, correct the source of truth, then verify using the original reproduction.

title: Helm release deployed but Pods fail
aliases: helm release deployed but pods fail
summary: Evidence-first diagnostic path for Helm release deployed but Pods fail. Confirm scope, preserve evidence, isolate the failing layer, then remediate only after the observed condition is understood.

steps.title: Check Kubernetes state
steps.look: Determine whether the failure is runtime or release-state related.

steps.title: Review events
steps.look: Look for image, scheduling, admission, mount or readiness failures.

steps.title: Inspect Helm release
steps.look: Check release status, revision and hooks.

steps.title: Inspect installed manifest
steps.look: Compare installed resources with intended configuration.

likely_causes: For “Helm release deployed but Pods fail”: kubelet/runtime/networking is unhealthy or cannot report to the API server.
Disk/inode/memory/PID pressure triggers node conditions or eviction.
Certificates, heartbeat/lease, OS/runtime or local network/storage configuration is degraded.
verification: Node Ready remains True and pressure conditions False.
Affected Pods stop being evicted/recreated.
Kubelet/runtime and workload networking/storage remain healthy over time.
escalation: Node Conditions/events and Lease timing
Kubelet/runtime logs
Disk/inode/memory/PID usage and affected Pod inventory

branches.when: Ready is Unknown or heartbeat stale
branches.then: Check kubelet/runtime connectivity and Lease timing.

branches.when: A pressure condition is True
branches.then: Quantify that resource and identify consumers.

branches.when: Only one node is affected
branches.then: Compare runtime/CNI/DNS/filesystem/kubelet with a healthy node.

example.root_cause: The walkthrough isolates “Helm release deployed but Pods fail” to the first live state/dependency that differs from the intended Kubernetes configuration.
example.remediation: Correct the owning manifest/controller/dependency at its source, apply the minimum safe change, and re-run the same diagnostic checks.
example.verification: Re-run the same checks, confirm the workload reaches its intended healthy/Ready state, and observe fresh events/logs through the original failure window.
example.lesson: Use the first concrete condition/event mismatch to narrow the incident; avoid changing several Kubernetes layers at once.
example.note: Simulated production-style example. Names, IDs and outputs are illustrative; verify commands and change policy in the real environment.
example.severity: Production-impacting example; simulated for training and troubleshooting guidance.
initial_hypotheses: For “Helm release deployed but Pods fail”: kubelet/runtime/networking is unhealthy or cannot report to the API server.
Disk/inode/memory/PID pressure triggers node conditions or eviction.
The visible symptom may be secondary, so preserve state and verify the failing layer before changing anything.
ruled_out: Do not assume the top-level status is the root cause.
Do not restart, delete, prune, force, broaden permissions, or change multiple layers merely to test a guess.
If the first diagnostic layer is healthy, explicitly move to the next dependency instead of forcing a fix at the healthy layer.
example.fix_decision: Choose the smallest source-of-truth correction that addresses the confirmed root cause. Prefer fixing the owning manifest, image/build definition, Compose configuration, Docker daemon configuration, or responsible dependency over one-off live mutations.
example.safety_and_rollback: Before a state-changing action, preserve the before-state, confirm the exact target/environment, identify the rollback path, and follow the project's change process. Commands shown in the walkthrough are illustrative; destructive remediation is intentionally not auto-executed.
success_criteria: The original symptom no longer reproduces.
The corrected state remains healthy through the same restart/load/failure window.
Fresh logs/events/status no longer contain the original failure signature.
example.transferable_pattern: Kubernetes pattern: start from the observable symptom, identify the first concrete mismatch in the Helm-Deployed Workloads path, prove the responsible layer with a second piece of evidence, correct the source of truth, then verify using the original reproduction.
